why: Turning back the fewest cars means keeping the longest subsequence in which each car weighs at most U and every two consecutive kept cars sum to at most U. That is an LIS-style DP: best[i] = 1 + max best[j] over earlier j with weight[j] <= U - weight[i], and a prefix-max Fenwick tree over compressed weights answers that max in O(log n).
hints: Minimise removals = maximise the cars you keep. What condition links a kept car to the kept car right before it?
dp[i] = longest valid kept sequence ending at car i = 1 + max dp[j] for j < i with weight[j] <= U - weight[i]. It is like LIS, but the comparison is against U - weight[i].
Compress weights; scan cars left to right; query the prefix max of dp over weights <= U - w with a Fenwick tree, then store dp at w. Skip cars heavier than U. Answer n - max dp. O(n log n).
pitfalls: A car heavier than U can never be kept, even alone.
The condition is on consecutive kept cars only, not on all pairs, so it is not enough to keep the lightest cars.
The O(n^2) DP is the right idea but too slow for large n; the Fenwick prefix max fixes that.
constraints:
• Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds: 1 ≤ weight.length ≤ 10^5
  • 1 ≤ weight[i], U ≤ 10^9
